video.title: 4 Tips For Consistently Crushing Slow Balls

classification.reason: The coach presents four core technical principles to attack slow floating balls with a student demonstrating right and wrong mechanics.

problem.title_as_question: How can players consistently attack and crush slow balls?
problem.definition: Slow balls lack forward court penetration and drop straight down, requiring players to actively generate front-to-back penetration with positive balance, appropriate hand height, early reaction, and precise ball tracking.
prerequisites: Ability to track and dink slow balls back over the net

symptoms.description: Players fail to crush or attack slow floaters with consistency, struggling to put the ball away.
The player stays in place while swinging, with the back foot landing at or behind its starting position.
The racket hand prepares far below ball level, producing erratic drives or accidental moonballs.
The player contacts the ball low around knee height rather than above net level.
The player swings blindly through an arbitrary point in the air without clear awareness of the ball's location.

causes.statement: Slow balls do not penetrate through the court and drop straight down, requiring the hitter to supply all front-to-back penetration.
Players attempt to attack while remaining static in place rather than moving their back foot forward into positive balance.
Players prepare their hand way below the incoming ball to brush topspin instead of matching hand height to drive flatter.
Players react late to short balls, allowing them to drop low below net height where attacking is no longer viable.
Players fail to watch the ball hit the court because its slow pace feels unthreatening, losing track of its exact position in space.

angles.summary: Positive balance requires the back foot to land ahead of its starting position to drive court penetration.
Fast balls extend the contact zone by coming through the court, whereas slow balls drop straight down without penetration.
Coach has the demonstrator deliberately hit from a static stance to illustrate how unnatural staying in place looks.
Wearing a resistance band around the waist imparts the physical feeling of driving forward through the back leg.
Coach corrects the urge to drop the hand low for topspin, explaining that driving flatter requires matching hand height to ball height.
Coach debunks the idea that slow balls can be tracked passively, showing that players must actively watch the bounce to coordinate contact.

solutions.summary: Attach a resistance band around the waist and hit drop-fed balls while pressing forward against the band's resistance.
solutions.external_goal: Press forward against the resistance of the band while hitting drop-fed balls.

solutions.summary: Without the resistance band, retain the physical sensation of driving through the shot with the back leg.
Look at the ball's incoming height and actively prepare your hand at the height of the ball to drive flatter.
solutions.external_goal: Prepare hand level with the incoming ball.

solutions.summary: Recognize the short floater early and sprint up to strike the ball while it is still two to three feet above the net.
solutions.external_goal: Strike the ball while it is two to three feet above net height.

solutions.summary: Watch the incoming slow ball make contact with the court surface so you can see it rise cleanly and swing with intention.
solutions.external_goal: Watch the ball hit the ground.
